claims.text: Animal protein intake was not associated with all-cause mortality after adjusting for major lifestyle and dietary risk factors.
Animal protein intake was associated with higher cardiovascular mortality.
Plant protein intake was associated with lower all-cause mortality.
Plant protein intake was associated with lower cardiovascular mortality.
The mortality associations of animal and plant protein intake were confined to participants with at least one unhealthy lifestyle factor.
Substituting 3% of energy from plant protein for protein from processed red meat was associated with lower all-cause mortality.
Substituting 3% of energy from plant protein for protein from unprocessed red meat was associated with lower all-cause mortality.
Substituting 3% of energy from plant protein for protein from egg was associated with lower all-cause mortality.

evidence.description: HR of 1.02 per 10% energy increment (95% CI, 0.98-1.05; P for trend = .33) for animal protein intake and all-cause mortality.
HR of 1.08 per 10% energy increment (95% CI, 1.01-1.16; P for trend = .04) for animal protein intake and cardiovascular mortality.
HR of 0.90 per 3% energy increment (95% CI, 0.86-0.95; P for trend < .001) for plant protein intake and all-cause mortality.
HR of 0.88 per 3% energy increment (95% CI, 0.80-0.97; P for trend = .007) for plant protein intake and cardiovascular mortality.

Associations were confined to participants with at least 1 unhealthy lifestyle factor (smoking, heavy alcohol intake, overweight/obesity, physical inactivity) and not evident among those without any risk factors.
HR for all-cause mortality was 0.66 (95% CI, 0.59-0.75) when 3% energy from plant protein was substituted for processed red meat protein.
HR for all-cause mortality was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.84-0.92) when 3% energy from plant protein was substituted for unprocessed red meat protein.
HR for all-cause mortality was 0.81 (95% CI, 0.75-0.88) when 3% energy from plant protein was substituted for egg protein.

methodologies.name: Prospective cohort analysis with repeated dietary assessment
methodologies.description: Prospective cohort analysis evaluating animal and plant protein intake via regularly updated validated food frequency questionnaires.
conditions: Nurses' Health Study follow-up: 1980 to June 1, 2012
Health Professionals Follow-up Study follow-up: 1986 to January 31, 2012

limitations.text: Defining what represents a macronutritionally balanced diet remains an open question in nutrition research.
Observed mortality associations were not evident among individuals without any unhealthy lifestyle risk factors.
